faqs.a: Both land within a few percent for 1-10 reps. Epley runs slightly high, Brzycki slightly low at higher reps. Averaging them, as this calculator does, is the pragmatic choice most coaches use.
faqs.q: Which formula is more accurate, Epley or Brzycki?

faqs.a: 3-8 reps to near-failure gives the best estimate. Singles are the most accurate but risky; sets past 12 reps make both formulas drift.
faqs.q: How many reps should I use for the estimate?

faqs.a: Strength: 85-95% for low reps. Muscle growth: 65-85%. Endurance and technique: 50-65%. The table above your result lists them all.

faqs.q: Why is my estimated 1RM higher than what I can actually lift?

one-rep-max-calculator.formula:
Epley: 1RM = W x (1 + R / 30)
Brzycki: 1RM = W x 36 / (37 - R)

Example: 80 kg x 8 reps
Epley: 80 x (1 + 8/30) = 80 x 1.2667 = 101.3 kg
Brzycki: 80 x 36 / (37 - 8) = 80 x 36/29 = 99.3 kg
Average: (101.3 + 99.3) / 2 = 100.3 kg
howTo: Enter the weight you lifted (bar included).
Enter the reps you did to near-failure with good form.
Your Epley, Brzycki, and averaged 1RM appear instantly.
Use the percentage table below to pick training loads.
Retest every 8-12 weeks - or just recalculate when your sets get stronger.
keyFacts: 1RM = the most weight you can lift once with good form.
Formulas are most accurate for 1-10 reps; past 12 they drift.
Use 65-85% of 1RM for most muscle-building training, 85%+ for strength.
Always warm up and use a spotter before testing near your max.

one-rep-max-calculator.quickAnswer: Your one-rep max is roughly what you lift times a factor for your reps. Lifting 80 kg for 8 reps gives about 101.3 kg by Epley (weight x (1 + reps/30)) and 99.3 kg by Brzycki (weight x 36/(37 - reps)) - an average of about 100.3 kg. Both are estimates; a true 1RM needs a real test.
